# Britain's House of Lords Suspends Two Members Amid Corruption Scandal

LONDON, England (CNN) -- In a historic ruling on Wednesday, Britain's House of Lords voted to suspend two of its members over corruption allegations—marking the first time in nearly four centuries that a peer has been barred from the chamber. A spokesman for the House confirmed that no lord had faced such a sanction since 1642.

Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott stand accused of agreeing to leverage their parliamentary influence to insert a loophole into proposed tax legislation in exchange for payment. Unbeknownst to them, the individual offering the bribe was an undercover journalist.

The scheme was uncovered through a sting operation conducted by The Sunday Times, in which reporters posed as representatives of a foreign business seeking to establish a retail chain in the United Kingdom. According to the newspaper, secret recordings captured Lord Truscott, a former energy minister, discussing a fee of up to $113,000 to work "behind the scenes" on the lobbyists' behalf. Lord Taylor, meanwhile, allegedly offered to lobby ministers and officials for an annual retainer of $189,000. The newspaper noted, however, that "neither peer took any money or offered to introduce an amendment themselves."

Truscott and Taylor were among four members of the House of Lords investigated by the chamber's Sub-Committee on Interests. Last week, the ethics panel concluded that Truscott had been "advertising his power and willingness to influence parliament in order for substantial financial inducement." Truscott denounced the finding as "outrageous and slanderous," according to the panel's official report, which subsequently rejected his appeal.

Taylor, for his part, maintained that he had recognized the sting operation from the outset and had made "increasingly extravagant and outlandish claims in an effort to 'flush out' the truth," the official Lords report stated. The ethics committee, however, deemed his explanation "full of internal contradictions" and concluded that he had violated the Lords Code of Conduct.

Two other lawmakers implicated in the investigation, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape, were cleared of any wrongdoing.

The suspensions of Truscott and Taylor stem officially from breaches of the Code of Conduct, which mandates that members "always act on their personal honor." London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that neither peer will face criminal charges. Their suspension will remain in effect until the next parliamentary session convenes in November; only the Queen holds the authority to permanently revoke a lord's title.

Both Taylor and Truscott are affiliated with the governing Labour Party. Lord Taylor has served in the House of Lords, parliament's upper chamber, since 1978, while Lord Truscott was granted his peerage in 2004.

This unprecedented suspension comes just one day after the Speaker of the House of Commons—parliament's lower chamber—was compelled to resign, the first such departure in over 300 years.

*CNN's Nicola Goulding contributed to this report.*

# The Lords "Cash for Amendments" Scandal: A Historic Reckoning

In January 2009, the British House of Lords found itself at the center of an unprecedented scandal that would ultimately lead to the most severe disciplinary action taken against its members in over three centuries. The controversy erupted following an undercover investigation conducted by journalists from The Sunday Times, who employed a classic sting operation to expose potential corruption within the upper chamber of Parliament.

## The Sting Operation

The investigative journalists posed as representatives of a fictitious foreign business seeking to influence legislation, presenting themselves as lobbyists with a specific interest in securing favorable changes to British tax law. They approached several members of the House of Lords, ostensibly seeking assistance in navigating the legislative process. Among those who responded to these overtures were Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott, two peers who allegedly expressed willingness to leverage their positions and influence within Parliament.

According to the recordings and evidence gathered during the operation, both peers were captured discussing their ability to help insert a specific tax loophole into pending legislation. Crucially, these discussions reportedly included conversations about substantial fees the peers would expect to receive in exchange for their assistance—raising serious questions about the potential for lawmakers to be improperly influenced by financial incentives from outside interests.

## The Investigation and Its Findings

The revelations, once published, sent shockwaves through Westminster and prompted immediate calls for a thorough investigation. The House of Lords, recognizing the gravity of the allegations and their implications for public trust in the institution, launched a formal inquiry into the conduct of the implicated peers. This investigation examined whether Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott had violated the Code of Conduct governing the behavior and ethical obligations of members of the House of Lords.

The Code of Conduct, which outlines the standards expected of peers, explicitly prohibits members from using their position for personal financial gain in ways that could compromise the integrity of the legislative process. The investigation sought to determine whether the peers' alleged willingness to accept payment in exchange for legislative influence constituted a clear breach of these established ethical guidelines.

## A Historic Verdict

Following the investigation, the House of Lords reached a landmark decision: both Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott would be suspended from the chamber. This ruling carried extraordinary historical weight, as it marked the first time since 1642—during the tumultuous period of the English Civil War—that a member of the House of Lords had been formally barred from participating in the chamber's proceedings.

The significance of this decision cannot be overstated. For more than 360 years, the House of Lords had not taken such drastic action against its own members, making this suspension a truly historic moment in British parliamentary history. The vote to suspend the two peers represented a clear signal that the House of Lords was prepared to hold its members accountable to rigorous ethical standards, even when doing so required unprecedented disciplinary measures.

## Broader Implications

This episode served as a watershed moment for the House of Lords, an institution often criticized for being resistant to reform and insulated from the kind of accountability mechanisms applied to other branches of government. The willingness of peers to investigate and ultimately punish their own colleagues demonstrated a commitment to preserving the integrity of the legislative process and maintaining public confidence in the chamber's ethical standards.

The scandal also reignited broader debates about the adequacy of oversight mechanisms within the House of Lords and raised questions about whether additional reforms might be necessary to prevent similar incidents in the future. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Parliament to external attempts at influence-peddling and underscored the importance of robust ethical safeguards to protect against corruption.

Ultimately, the suspension of Lord Taylor of Blackburn and Lord Truscott stood as a powerful reminder that even long-standing institutions steeped in tradition could be compelled to adapt and enforce accountability when faced with clear evidence of misconduct—setting an important precedent for how the House of Lords would address ethical violations in the years that followed.
